en: The Kṣṇayamāri Tantra, Chapter One.
Homage to the Three Jewels!
Homage to the glorious Kṛṣṇayamāri! Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling within the wombs (*bhaga*) of all the Vajra Ladies of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas,
together with Mohavajrayamāri, Piśunavajrayamāri, Rāgavajrayamāri, Īrṣyāvajrayamāri, Dveṣavajrayamāri, Mudgarayamāri, Daṇḍayamāri, Padmayamāri, and Khaḍgayamāri.
And with Vajracarcikā, Vajravārāhī, Vajrasarasvatī, and Vajragaurī;
thus, with the great hosts of Yamāris headed by these [deities]. (1)
Then the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi addressed Vajrasattva, the Lord of all Tathāgatas.
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, emitted from the space-vajras and from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the samādhi named "Vajra that Severes All Māras. 2.
By means of the practice of Candravajra, one should meditate on Yamaghātaka;
for the sake of pacifying the Māras, he shall dispel hatred in every way. (3)
For the sake of protection, one should visualize a vajra filled with five-colored rays;
by means of that vajra, one should likewise create the ground, the enclosure, the wall, and the cage. (4)

Then the Blessed One, the progenitor of all Tathāgatas, entered the samādhi called "Vajra that Shatters All Māras" and emitted from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind this seed-syllable of the Noble Lady of the Vajra of Universal Delusion and so forth. // 5 //

In the midst of *ya*, *ma*, *dha*, *kṣa*, *sa*, *maṃ*, *da*, *ya*, *ca*, *ni*, *rā*, *jā*, *sa*, *do*, *ru*, *ṇa*, *yo*, and *ni*—the letter *ra* at the beginning of *yamadhna* is [present]; when there is the letter *kṣe*, delusion (*moha*) is said to occur. (6)
In the syllable *sa* is said to be *piśuna* (malicious speech), and in the syllable *ma*, *rāga* (passion);
in the syllable *da* as well, there is *īrṣyā* (envy)— these five are proclaimed as the slayers of Yama.
In the syllable *ya* is known Mudgara; in the syllable *ca* is Daṇḍanāyaka; in the syllable *ni* is Padmapāṇi; and in the syllable *rā* is Khaḍgavān as well. (8)
Carcikā is proclaimed in the syllable *ja*, Vārāhī in the syllable *sa*, Sarasvatī in the syllable *da*, and Gaurī is remembered in the syllable *ru*. // 9 //
In the four corners of the womb [maṇḍala], the four agents are considered to reside;
one should contemplate the terrifying Viśvavajra situated in the center of the space-vajra. 10.
One should meditate on Kāladāruṇa situated in the center of Yamāntaka;
at the eastern gate, Mohavajra, and at the southern [gate], Piśuna. (11)
In the west, one should visualize Rāgavajra; likewise, in the north, that called Īrṣyā; and in the corners, on the four-pronged vajras, one should visualize Carcikā and the others. 12.
One should visualize the mallet and other implements upon the four-pronged vajra at the gates;
in the four corners of the double-vajra (viśvavajra), there are four human skulls. // 13 //
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, entered the samādhi called Yamārivajra and uttered this mantra of the great family of hatred:
OṂ HRĪḤ ṢTRĪḤ VIKṚTĀNANA HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. // 14 //
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the mantra of Delusion-Vajra: Oṃ vijajik. 15.
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the Piśuna-vajra mantra:
Oṃ Ratnadhṛk. 16.
Then indeed, the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the passion-vajra mantra:
Oṃ ārolik. 17.
Then indeed, the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the envy-vajra mantra:
Oṃ prajñādhṛk. 18.
Then indeed, the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the Mudgara-vajra mantra:
Oṃ mudgaradhṛk. 19.
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the staff-vajra mantra:
Oṃ daṇḍadhṛk. (20)
Then indeed, the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the Padma-vajra mantra:
Oṃ padmadhṛk. // 21 //
Then indeed the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the sword-vajra mantra:
Oṃ khaḍgadhṛk. // 22 //
Then indeed the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the Vajracarcikā mantra:
Oṃ moharati. (23)
Then indeed, the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the mantra of Vajravārāhī:
Oṃ dveṣarati. 24.
Then indeed, the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the Vajrasarasvatī mantra:
Oṃ rāgarati. 25.
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the Vajragaurī mantra:
Oṃ vajrarati. (26)
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, uttered the mantra for the empowerment of body, speech, and mind: *oṃ sarvatathāgatakāyavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas. Oṃ, I am of the nature of the mind-vajra of all Tathāgatas. // 27 //
Then indeed, the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, manifested the great embodiment of hatred. 28.
The wise one should meditate upon Yamāri, who has three faces, six arms, and is wrathful with a luster like that of sapphire; having manifested the vajra in his hand. (29)
Having visualized [the deity] with three faces, six arms, peaceful, and possessing a radiance like a clear reflection,
and having visualized a wheel in his hand, one should visualize the Mohavajra.
One should visualize [the deity] with three faces and six arms, whose back has the luster of molten gold;
having visualized a jewel in the hand, one should then visualize the Piśuna-vajra.
Three-faced and six-armed, subduing, with a radiance equal to a ruby;
having visualized a lotus in his hand, one should visualize Rāgavajra. (32)
One should visualize [the deity] with three faces and six arms, entirely resembling an emerald stone;
having visualized a sheath in the hand, one should visualize the Īrṣyāvajra.
Thus ends the first chapter, on Abhisamaya, in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayāmaritantra*.
The Second Chapter.
Then, indeed, all the Blessed Tathāgatas praised the Blessed Mahāvajrasattva. (1)
You are the nature of the vajra of delusion, Yamāri, most terrifying;
you consist of all Buddhas, you are peaceful—homage to you, Kāyavajra! // 2 //
You are the nature of Piśunavajra, Yamāri, most terrifying;
resembling Cittavajra, O Ratnavajra, homage be to you! 3.
You are the nature of passion-vajra, Yamāri, most terrifying;
O supreme among all excellent sounds, Vāgvajra, homage be to you! 4.
You are Yamāri, whose nature is the vajra of envy, the performer of all rites;
you resemble the body-vajra, with a sword in hand—homage be to you! (5)
You are the self-nature of all Buddhas, the singular synthesis of all Buddhas;
O supreme among the most excellent of all Buddhas, Lord of the Mandala, homage be to you! (6)

"Vajra-eye, vajra-ear, vajra-nose, vajra-tongue, vajra-body, vajra-speech, and vajra-mind," so said the Blessed One; this is the samaya of the empowerment of the eyes and the other sense organs. // 7 //
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the terrible maṇḍala of Yamāri, which has the appearance of the Slayer of Yama and accomplishes all desires and goals. (8)
The wise one should trace the mandala of Yamadhana with a new, well-prepared, beautiful, and well-measured thread.
Complete with all characteristics and destroying all obstacles,
the mandala is shaped like a mandala according to the measurements for rites of pacification and the rest. (10)
One should draw a karma-vajra there, with five prongs on all sides;
in its center, one should draw a vajra filled with vajra-flames. (11)
In the eastern spoke, one should draw a wheel crowded with wheel-rays;
in the southern [spoke], one should draw a jewel crowded with garlands of rays.
To the west, one should draw a lotus with a radiance equal to a ruby;
to the north, one should draw a sword filled with manifold flames. // 13 //
In the eastern corner one should draw a wheel; in the south, one should draw a vajra;
and in the west, a lotus flower with its stalk, its face fully blossomed.
To the north is a yellow lotus, possessing a radiance equal to five rays of light. // 14 //
At the eastern gate, a mallet; likewise, a staff at the southern;
a lotus at the western gate; and one holding a sword and a vajra at the northern.
Having recognized the mandala as perfected, one should perform worship in particular;
one should worship the Buddhas with the five qualities of sensory pleasure, free from hesitation. (16)
Thus ends the second chapter, the Great Maṇḍala Chapter, in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
[Page 18] Now, the third chapter:
then all the Blessed Ones from every direction made this request with this King of Praises. 1.
"O Lord, let the mandala that destroys all sins be drawn—the formidable Yamāntaka-maṇḍala, the leader of all maṇḍalas. (2)
Then the Blessed One, Mahāvajradhara, brought forth from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the commitment of tasting the nectar:
OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ. 3.
Through the application of the tongue-vajra, there is the pleasing of all Vajradharas,
having caused all the Perfectly Awakened Ones to enter in their own forms as the aspects of gnosis. (4)

One should visualize [the deity] established in meditative absorption as being drawn forth, entered, bound, and likewise brought under control by means of the four mantras beginning with *mudgara*. (5)
Having visualized the buffalo-vajra, one should visualize the Lord of the Mandala;
situated in the center of the clear mandala, one should visualize the delusion-vajra. // 6 //
One should contemplate the one called Piśuna situated in the middle of the seventh group of seven;
one should meditate upon Rāgavajrin situated in the center of a red maṇḍala.
One should meditate upon the Karma-vajrin situated in the center of the karma-maṇḍala. // 7 //
In pacifying rites, however, there is Mohavajra; likewise, Piśuna in enriching rites;
in subjugating rites, indeed, by means of Rāgavajra; and in all cases, by means of Karmavajra. // 8 //
Human oil placed in a human skull, a wick made from human hair, and soot produced in a cremation ground through the application of the *karmavajra* ritual—[these are the materials]. (9)

One should cultivate the rite upon the ointment, and likewise upon the one who applies the ointment; by this application of mantra-repetition, the accomplishment of the ointment shall be attained. // 10 //
One should prepare a foot-ointment with saffron and secret blood;
through the application of the Karma-vajra, success is achieved by means of this foot-ointment. // 11 //
Having taken the five nectars together with the five meats, and having encased them with the three metals, one achieves success through the application of ritual action. // 12 //
One should accomplish a sword made of magnetite through the application of ritual action;
by means of the practice of the Action-Vajra, the Action-Sword is perfected. // 13 //
Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on the Application of Ritual Actions, in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
[Page 22] The fourth chapter.
Then all the Blessed Tathāgatas requested the Blessed Mahāvajradhara with this King of Praises. // 1 //
How do sentient beings proceed according to the various divisions and sub-divisions of their karma?
Tell us, O Great Vajra; may those who are oceans of wisdom listen! // 2 //
Then King Vajradhara, the accomplisher of all activities, whose very nature is the healing of all defects, spoke these words: (3)

Then indeed, all the Blessed Tathāgatas, having performed worship manifested by the mind-vajra, prostrated, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and bowed down again and again, listened to the words of the Blessed One. 4.
Then King Vajradhara proclaimed the subjugating yantra: "Among all these yantras, there has never been one such as this, nor will there ever be. (5)
It should be performed for the sake of subduing women and likewise for protection; for pacifying rites, one should take yellow pigment (rocanā) and write upon birch bark or bamboo bark.
Having drawn two wheels, one should interlace the mantra "namo namaḥ" within them,
inside a pair of joined shallow bowls that are free from the root of black mustard and other such substances.
Having placed it in the midst of ghee and honey, one should wrap it with a white thread;
facing the east, one should worship it with white flowers at the three junctions of the day.
Having meditated upon oneself as Yamāntaka, with the luster of a moonstone, one should place it before oneself;
then, seeing the person to be accomplished mounted upon a moon disc, one should consecrate them. // 9 //
Seeing [the deity] being sprinkled by numerous perfectly awakened Buddhas with white jars, radiant as the moon and filled with the five nectars, one should begin the recitation. (10)
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā / Oṃ, homage to Devadatta! Bring peace, homage, svāhā! Thus he proclaimed the pledge of the rite for pacification (*śāntika*). 11.

For men, however, the two wheels should be written with saffron in rites for pacification (śāntika), and likewise with saffron in rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika); the insertion of the name [of the person] should be done with the word "svāhā. (12)
Having taken the name of the person to be accomplished, one should cast it into clarified butter and honey;
having placed it within a pair of earthen saucers, one should encircle it with a yellow thread.
Facing north, one should worship at the three junctions of the day with yellow flowers;
indeed, one should visualize oneself as being of yellow color and as the destroyer of Yama.
One should visualize the object of accomplishment situated upon a beautiful yellow moon and bathe it with yellow jars;
having meditated upon the consecration, one should recite the mantra while vibrating with light to effect nourishment (*puṣṭika*). // 15 //

Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. Oṃ laṃ, grant nourishment (*puṣṭi*) to Devadatta, grant it, svāhā; or *vauṣaṭ*. Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā *vauṣaṭ*; grant nourishment to Devadatta, *vauṣaṭ* hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Samaya of Prosperity. // 16 //
[26] On birch bark or even on a cloth, with lac juice,
or with red sandalwood, or indeed with the blood from the ring finger; 17.
Having drawn two wheels, one should interlace them with the syllable *ho*;
[this should be done] upon a yantra devoid of time and other such factors, within the cavity formed by two joined shallow bowls.
One should wrap clarified butter filled with honey with a red thread;
standing facing west, one should worship it with red flowers. // 19 //
One should visualize oneself as Yamaghātaka, red in color with great flames, mounted upon a red moon; and one should likewise visualize the person to be subdued in the same manner. // 20 //

Visualizing oneself attracting the object of accomplishment with red rays of light issuing from one's own body, which have the appearance of being red, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times. // 21 //
One should perform the recitation while contemplating that the target is indeed distressed, fallen like a cripple, naked, and with disheveled hair. (22)
[27] If he does not come, the practitioner must heat that machine in a smokeless fire of khadira wood, having removed the ghee and other substances. 23.
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ hoḥ! Subdue Yajñadatta for Devadatta, hoḥ!
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā vauṣaṭ! Bring Yajñadatta under the control of Devadatta, vauṣaṭ! Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Samaya of Subjugation. 24.
Or else, having drawn two wheels upon a cloth from a cemetery or upon a rag smeared with earth by oneself, using lac mixed with red pigment; 25.
One should interweave the name with the syllable *jaḥ* and the syllable *hrīḥ*;
having placed a woman within a lotus-vessel or a casket, one should worship her. // 26 //
Having encircled it with red thread, one should worship it with red flowers;
one should visualize oneself as Yamaghātaka, red in color and resembling the sun at its zenith. (27)
One should also visualize the person to be subdued as red in color, pierced in the heart by goads and bound at the neck with nooses. (28)
One should visualize [the deity] mounted upon a red lion, joined with the wind-mandala, being sprinkled with the five substances, and approaching. // 29 //
When the one to be accomplished does not come, the practitioner should heat that machine;
once a fire of khadira wood is kindled, he should commence the recitation there.
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ hrīḥ, summon [Name]! Hrīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! Hrīḥ! Thus spoke the Blessed One; this is the Samaya of Summoning. // 31 //
On two pieces of cloth, the wise one should draw two wheels with saffron juice and embellish them with the syllable *laṃ*.
Having taken the name of the person to be accomplished and placed it within a pair of shallow bowls,
the wise practitioner should place it upon a yellow bowl and draw a line there.
Having drawn seven or four lines with a concentrated mind,
one should then draw Mount Sumeru with its eight peaks upon them.
One should interlace the syllable *hūṃ* and the syllable *vaṃ* to form Mount Meru;
above that, one should draw the maṇḍala of Mahendra with the syllable *laṃ*.
One should visualize oneself as Yamāntaka, yellow in color, trampled by a double-vajra (viśvavajra), and encircled by a yellow thread. // 36 //
Facing south, the yogin, established within the maṇḍala of Mahendra, should visualize the object of practice as yellow and quickly place him as being trampled by mountains. // 37 //

One should visualize the target as being trampled by the Viśvavajra situated below the Maheśvara maṇḍala, and further oppressed by formidable mountains such as Mandara, which resemble the Snowy Mountains; there, one should perform the recitation. (38)
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ laṃ! Paralyze the place of Devadatta, laṃ!
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Samaya of Paralysis. (39)
One who desires the paralysis of speech should likewise draw two wheels;
having interlaced the names of the target [to be subdued] within them, one should then clearly recite the mantra. (40)

Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ laṃ! For Devadatta, when he performs whatever task has been undertaken, for Yajñadatta who obstructs it and speaks deviously, perform the paralysis of speech! Laṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Samaya of Speech-Paralysis. (41)
This task, as described, must be performed with extreme secrecy;
through the yoga of Kṛṣṇayamāri, success shall be attained in a single day.
The practitioner should draw two wheels upon a cloth from a cemetery,
using black mustard seeds, salt, poison, and nimba.
The three pungents, mustard oil, and charcoal from a cremation ground, along with the resin of *dhuttūra* leaves and likewise *caṇḍa* seeds; (44)
Taking blood from the ring finger, or with the juice of the *citraka* plant, and having taken saline soil and the collyrium from a Caṇḍāla’s vessel; 45.
On the fourteenth day of the waning moon, when one is hungry and possesses a sharp stylus, the practitioner,
with a cruel mind for the sake of subduing the wicked, should draw [the diagram] at midday. (46)
One should interweave the name of the being to be destroyed with the syllable *huṃ*;
facing south, the yogin should visualize himself as Yamaghātaka. (47)
He has a wrathful form, is exceedingly fierce, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads; he stands upon a buffalo, has a lolling tongue, a large belly, and is terrifying.
With tawny hair blazing upwards, and likewise with brownish beard and eyebrows;
in his right hand he holds a great vajra, and in the second [hand] a sword.
In the third [hand], one should now draw a sickle in the left;
likewise, a wheel, a great lotus, and a skull-bowl on the left.
The primary face is that of a great bee; the right is said to be of brilliant wheel-like luster, and the left is like blood-red in color, adorned with vajra ornaments.
From the great opening of the pore of his skin, he should emanate the Lord of his own family,
standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a solar disc above. (52)

Having thus armored oneself, one should visualize the object of practice (sādhya) before oneself, with a mouth made terrifying by distorted fangs and resembling the fire of the doomsday conflagration. 53.
Soiled, decrepit, struck down by diseases and deformed limbs, naked, trembling, distressed, and covered with wounds upon the body. (54)
Those covered with goiters and swellings, mangled by weapons, afflicted by cold winds, and cast into the midst of fire; // 55 //
While that great evildoer was being devoured by buffaloes, tigers, and long-snouted dogs, he was terrified by the army of the Buddha. (56)
[34] Standing in the midst of the belly of Death, their bodies covered with thorns,
they are trampled by feet bound in shackles and fetters, and likewise cut into pieces.
One should meditate on [the victim] as rendered homeless (or supportless), smeared with black mustard and salt;
uttering the sound "śīt," one should meditate for the protection of that person's body. 58.

One should cause his armor to burst asunder and contemplate him as having a body that is void, by means of the wrathful deities arising from one's own body—namely, Yamāntaka and the forms of the Noble Ones. (59)
There, one should visualize [the victim] being slaughtered, drinking fat and marrow;
and in front of him, one should meditate upon Yama, holding a staff in his hand and possessing great strength.
One should contemplate that evil person as having been slain by that [deity] there;
taking his intestinal cord, vultures go toward the sky. (61)

[The practitioner] should contemplate that the one to be converted is being dragged into the underworld by nāgas, tormented by urinary stones and other ailments; or else, with a mind permeated by compassion, he should contemplate the one to be converted in this way. (62)
He causes [beings] to transcend cyclic existence and is born in the Buddha-fields.
Then indeed, all the Blessed Tathāgatas, with joyful minds, uttered these words: // 63 //
Oh, indeed, what is called "killing" is neither killing nor non-killing; for since one is liberated from evils, he who is killed is not truly killed at all. // 64 //

Having committed thousands of evils, one would dwell in the Avīci hell and other such realms; yet how great is the majesty of the Bound One (Baddha)! Even one who has been slain may attain awakening. 65.
Having generated even greater compassion, one should slay that which destroys sentient beings.
Oh, how divine is the power of compassion! One devoid of compassion does not attain success. // 66 //

Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Kill, kill Devadatta! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Conceptualization, regarding the mantra-tantra of the *ghāta*-vajra machine for killing and other such rites. (67)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, the commitment concerning the rites of killing and so forth, the manual, mantras, and tantra of Kṛṣṇayamāri, the embodiment of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
Fifth Chapter:
Likewise, having drawn two wheels, one should enclose them with the syllable *phaṭ*.
Having taken the name of the person to be accomplished, one should place it within a hollowed-out skull-cup. // 1 //
Having wrapped it with a blue thread, one should bury it in cremation grounds at the time of midday. // 2 //
Having taken hold of Śrīyamāri, one should indeed place the two objects of accomplishment (sādhya) in front;
the two objects of accomplishment are mounted upon a horse and a buffalo, holding weapons in their hands. // 3 //
One should contemplate the two sides through signs consisting of a multitude of wrathful forms;
both, indeed, are engaged in combat with minds possessed by anger.
Meditating upon the two wrathful powers as cultivated, one should begin the practice.
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Cause Devadatta to be estranged from Yajñadatta! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Samaya of Estrangement. (5)
Having drawn the two wheels according to that same previous procedure,
one should place them within a hollowed skull-cup, interspersed with the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
Having wrapped it with a black thread, one should bury it in a cemetery;
having assumed the Yamāri-yoga, one should visualize the victim before oneself. // 7 //
One should visualize a great blue-colored camel upon a black wind-maṇḍala shaped like a bow. // 8 //
Even for a Buddha, it is not possible to succeed against that great evildoer who has mounted it, being led toward the southern direction and struck by hosts of wrathful deities.
"Joṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ, O you of distorted face, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Expel Devadatta, hūṃ phaṭ! Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Samaya of Great Exorcism. 10.
The enraged yogin, with a face turned toward the south, [should act] with his own blood and funeral ashes, with poison, salt, black mustard, oil, and the water of a wild plantain tree. // 11 //
On a cloth from a cemetery, one should draw these two wheels in sequence:
for killing, they should be situated within the body of Yama; for causing enmity, within those of a buffalo and a horse.
For incitement, it resides in the body of a camel; for pacification, it is situated in the moon;
for nourishment, it is on a yellow moon; and for subjugation, it is in the hearts of women.

That which is situated in a goat is indeed praised for immobilization; that drawn from the center of Meru is likewise [effective] when situated in a śarabha or a lion—one should observe it thus in other cases as well. (14)
One should write [the mantra] on birch bark using yellow pigment (rocanā), lac, and especially saffron (kāśmīra); it will bring about subjugation (vaśya), there is no doubt of this. // 15 //
Having placed it in a pair of shallow bowls and held it with a virtuous mind,
one should inscribe it at midday using a pen made from a crow’s wing.

On the funeral pyre, within the lotuses of the *sampuṭa* [mudrā], by means of the application of oneself as Yamāntaka, one should repeat "Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ" and so forth; thus, the one to be subdued is situated on the right. (17)
The final *ya* of *śānta* and the *ya* of *nirdaya* are elided;
subsequently, the *ya* in the middle [of *nirdaya*] is also elided, and the remaining syllables are joined as desired. (18)
Having recited this *Karmaprasādhana* ten thousand times as a preliminary service, it should be performed by Jñānavajra through the application of Yamamāri. (19)
Furthermore, wherever this most terrible [mantra] is written down, even in that house there will be constant quarreling simply from the act of writing the syllables. (20)
Either on birch bark or even on a piece of cloth, with lac-dye or with red sandalwood,
or indeed with the blood from the ring finger.
Having drawn two wheels, one should encircle them with the syllable *hoḥ* within a yantra devoid of [the divisions of] time and so forth, enclosed between two shallow bowls (*śarāva*).
One should wrap clarified butter filled with honey with a red thread and worship it with red flowers while standing facing west.
One should visualize oneself as Yamaghātaka, red in color and blazing with great splendor,
mounted upon a red moon, and likewise visualize the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the same way.
Visualizing oneself drawing forth the object of accomplishment with rays of blood-red light in the form of hooks issuing from one's own body, one should clearly recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Having recited this mantra, which accomplishes all rites, ten thousand times as a preliminary service,
the one to be accomplished becomes overwhelmed and likewise falls at one's feet.
One should begin the recitation while visualizing [the deity] as radiant and with disheveled hair;
if the person to be subjugated does not come, the practitioner should heat that mantra.
Having prepared it without ghee and other such substances, [one should do so] in a smokeless fire of khadira wood.
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ hoḥ! Subdue Yajñadatta for Devadatta, hoḥ!
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ vauṣaṭ! Bring Yajñadatta under the control of Devadatta, vauṣaṭ!
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Lord of the Samaya.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Sequential Drawing of the Mandala," in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittarahasyakṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
[Page 43] The Sixth Chapter.

Then indeed, all the Blessed Tathāgatas requested the Blessed One, the Sovereign of all Tathāgatas, the Great Vajradhara, with this King of Praises: 1. "O Bhagavat, we request you, the Sovereign of all Tathāgatas, the Great Vajradhara."
The application of the regional mudrās is that by which the Vajradharas are pleased;
sealed with the vajra-mudrā, they bring about abundant accomplishment. // 2 //
Then King Vajradhara spoke these words:
"One should visualize the Yāmghna upon the heads of all those belonging to the maṇḍala. (3)
Constantly constructing the maṇḍala, one should always worship with fire-offerings (homa). One should always accomplish the commitments (samayas); let the vow (saṃvara) be thoroughly upheld. // 4 //
First is the crown initiation; second is from the tasting of the sword;
third is the vajra and bell; and fourth is the consumption of the moon. // 5 //
These four great empowerments issued from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa; by the power of these empowerments, the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Victors, [attain their state]. (6)
Now I shall proclaim the mantra for the ritual offering to all spirits;
when this great mantra is uttered, it causes all spirits to tremble. (7)
Oṃ indrāya hrīḥ, yamāya ṣṭrīḥ.
To Varuṇa, the syllable *viḥ*; to Kubera, the syllable *kṛḥ*; to Īśāna, the syllable *taḥ*.
To Agni in the east, to Nirṛti in the southwest, and to Vāyu in the northwest, [svāhā].
Hūṃ to Candra, hūṃ to Arka, phaṭ to Brahmā.
Vasudhārāyai phaṭ, Vemacitriṇe svā, Sarvabhūtebhyo hā.
Hā hā hī hī hūṃ hūṃ pheṃ pheṃ svāhā! // 8 //
Having fashioned a triangular mandala with substances mixed with feces, urine, and water,
the yogi should gratify the deities and then again recollect the sound "Hā-hā."
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, proclaimed the wheel of the expansion of activities. // 10 //
Having fashioned three mandalas of eight, twelve, or sixteen [squares],
the wise one, having drawn them according to the rule, should place the mantras everywhere.
The practitioner who observes the vow should place the perfected mantras within the twelfth square;
thus, the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, are brought to complete and total accomplishment. 12.
[47] He who is my king, he is my lord; he who is my protector, he is my refuge.
He who dwells in the night, he who dwells in the day, he who dwells in the fortnight, and he who dwells in the month. (13)
One should first place Yamadhyakṣa in the east, and Mañjuvajra in the south;
the syllable ME should be written in the west, and the tooth-stick in the north. (14)
Having taken the name of the one to be accomplished, one should place it in the void or in an intermediate direction;
having interlaced it with two *hūṃ*s, one should accomplish all tasks. // 15 //
And having written outside, beginning from the left, the mantra "yaśca nirājā sadoruṇa yonira" and so forth, one should accomplish it for the sake of all goals.
In the third square, in the square separated by one interval in front,
one should write, starting as before from the letter *ā*, the mantras beginning with *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ*.
One should likewise inscribe [the syllables] within the eight squares situated between those [previous ones]. // 17 //
"Make [him] mute, kill, expel, subjugate, cause enmity, bring peace, bring nourishment"—thus, according to the corresponding ritual action. // 18 //
The seed-syllables of the deities end with *namaḥ* or *namonta*, and at the conclusion are *vaṣaṭ* or *vauṣaṭ*;
when joined with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, they effect pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśa*), and so forth. (19)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Surveying of the Circle," in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
The seventh chapter:
[One should visualize the goddess] white, with three faces and six arms, holding a wheel in her hand, and possessing the luster of the moon.
The wise one, through the practice of attracting with red [light], should meditate upon Carcikā. // 1 //

The wise one should meditate upon Vārāhī—three-faced, six-armed, with a prominent nose, holding a vajra in her hand, and deep blue in color—by means of the practice for summoning through liquor. // 2 //

For the purpose of increasing wisdom, the practitioner should meditate upon Sarasvatī as red in color, with three faces and six arms, holding a lotus in her hand and possessing a serene countenance. (3)
The wise one should visualize Gaurī as having three faces, six arms, and a short stature, resembling an emerald-blue lotus, through the practice of attracting semen. (4)
Then the Blessed One, Mahāyamāntakavajra, entered the meditative absorption called the Vajra of Red Attraction and uttered this mantra of Vajracarcikā: // 5 //
Oṃ, Vajracarcikā, you who captivate the sapphire of the lords of siddhas; attract, attract the blood of those who harm the Triple Gem! Jaḥ! 6.
Having opened wide one's mouth, one should recollect this mantra;
the great jewel of the triple world will be drawn forth—of this there is no doubt. (7)
Then the Blessed One, Mahāyamārivajra, entered the meditative absorption called the Vajra of Attracting Liquor and uttered this Vajravārāhī mantra: // 8 //
Oṃ vajraghoṇe sughoṇe, O excellent Māmaki, summon, summon! Gather, gather! Draw forth the great liquor of the three realms! Jaḥ! // 9 //
Having fashioned a small vessel from clay the size of a hand, and having covered it,
one should joyfully recite the mantra while placing it upon a support known as *caurakeśa*. // 10 //
The majesty of this mantra was demonstrated in the city of Caityapattana;
by summoning courage and applying effort, the extraction of wine is successfully accomplished. (11)
Then the Blessed One, Mahāsamayamayadhvaja, entered the samādhi called Vajra of the Perfection of Wisdom and uttered this mantra of Vajrasarasvatī: 12. OṂ VAJRA-SARASVATI SVĀHĀ.
Oṃ picu picu, O increaser of wisdom! Blaze, blaze! O increaser of intelligence! Ghiri ghiri! O increaser of intellect! Svāhā! // 13 //
Having grasped it step by step from the first day until the full moon on all sides, one should begin to speak the refined language (saṃskṛta) in accordance with the moon. 14.
He shall attain the siddhi of the Yogīśvarī; he composes a hundred verses, and the entire threefold world-system is accomplished by him without exception or remainder. 15.
Then the Blessed One, Mahāyamāntakavajra, entered the samādhi called the Vajra for Attracting Semen and uttered this mantra of Vajragaurī for attracting semen: // 16 //
Oṃ kaṭṭini karṣaṇi gauri jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ hrīḥ, draw out the semen of the wicked and the most wicked, jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ hūṃ svāhā! // 17 //
Through the yoga of the wind-bell and the hook, from the mouth of the sky and the path of the vajra,
one should draw forth the mass of semen by means of the application of recitation and meditative cultivation. (18)
Whether in solitary forests or elsewhere, this rite impelled by karma is accomplished through a seven-night application; there is no doubt about this. (19)

Then the Blessed One, Mahāyamārivajra, entered the samādhi called "The Vajra that Cuts Time" and emitted this pledge of supreme consecration from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind. // 20 //
"O child, take these garlands of Audumbara, Māndāraka, Pārijāta, Tamālaka, and Karṇikāra flowers, and set forth."
O great sword of the triple world, honored by all the Buddhas, seize [it] as another sword of activity for the sake of conquering the Māras. 22.
[55] "O Child Vajra, take up the vajra and bell, which have the nature of wisdom and skillful means, for the sake of accomplishment; perform the gathering of disciples. (23)
This is indeed your precious drink, which perfects the vajra-body;
drink this mental water, my child, always with wisdom. 24.
The disciple drinks with ease for the sake of attaining the Slayer of Yama;
the Vajra-disciple brings excellence to the mind of the Great-Souled One. (25)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the application of summoning and other rites, in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
The Eighth Chapter.
Now, King Vajradhara, through the application of the protection wheel, [spoke].
And he spoke for the purpose of cutting down the wicked obstacles and impediments. // 1 //
I am King Khaḍgadhara; through the application of the protection wheel, I shatter with my blazing sword those born of the three bodies.
O Goddess, you are the witness for all those who follow the Buddhas;
O Yamaghni, as the master of the maṇḍala, I shall draw the maṇḍala. (3)
Having covered his face with a cloth at the door of the assembly hall, Kauśika said, "Who are you, sir? and he replied, "I am Subhaga."
Having placed a curtain between them, the wise disciple, with great devotion, should entreat the guru for the sake of initiation,
making the request three times. (5)
Just as the Buddhas [bestowed] great dharmas through the consecration of Vajrasattva, so too may you grant me a boon for the sake of my protection. (6)

The disciple should respectfully present song, instrumental music, worship, the water of honor (argha), and the water for the feet (pādya); or else, he should cause a hymn of praise to be performed there. // 7 //
Then King Vajradhara should recite the mantra of emptiness:
*Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas.*
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-dharmadhātu. // 8 //
[58] Now I shall explain the fire offering (homa), categorized according to pacification (śāntika) and other rites,
by means of which accomplishment (siddhi) shall arise that fulfills all ritual actions. 9.

In rites for pacification, one should act with a peaceful mind; in rites for nourishment, with a flourishing mind; in rites for subjugation, with an eager mind; and in rites for killing, with a distressed mind.
For pacification, the shape is circular; for enrichment, it is square;
for subjugation, it is called the half-moon; and for killing, it is like the element of space.
The length of the hand should be one cubit for pacification (śānti), and likewise two cubits for nourishment (pauṣṭika);
as it is for nourishment, so it is for subjugation (vaśya), while for killing (māraṇa) it should be twenty finger-breadths.

One should pierce for the purpose of the hand-measure: one cubit for pacification, one cubit for enrichment, two for killing, and five for subjugation; as it is for enrichment, so it is for subjugation. (13)

On the days of practice, one should perform a *śāntika* (pacifying) fire-sacrifice on the full moon day, a *pauṣṭika* (prosperity-inducing) sacrifice on the fourteenth day, and the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarman*) on the eighth day.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of Fire Offerings (*homa*), in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
The Ninth Chapter:
Having taken clay from the ocean, one should have a single nāga fashioned.
Having placed the syllable *oṃ phūḥ* at the heart, one should recite the mantra beginning with *hrīḥ ṣṛyā*. // 1 //
[64] Then, during a time of drought, one should cause rain to fall by means of ten thousand recitations (*ayutajāpa*).
One should mix the flesh of a black snake with *nimba* leaves. (2)
Having made a pill from that very [substance], the observer of the vow should cast it into the ocean; when recited ten thousand times, it is the supreme method for the stilling of waves. // 3 //
Taking one hundred seeds of *uṇḍa* mixed with black gram and rice, O God, by performing a fire oblation (*homa*) after reciting [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times, you shall be seen. // 4 //
The practitioner, observing the vow, should have an effigy made from the dregs of the cremation ground;
by anointing it with the juice of the *unmatta* plant ten thousand times, one suffers from leprosy.

By reciting the mantra four hundred thousand times with a collection of white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), one should perform the rite of awakening the sleeping; there is no doubt regarding the restoration of life. // 6 //
Having taken earth from a mountain cave, one should empower it with the *lakṣamantra*;
by merely wiping the head with it, headache is destroyed. // 7 //
Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, one should rub the head with the hand;
headache will not occur, it is destroyed—of this there is no doubt. // 8 //
One should fashion an image of Yamāri with two arms and one face, using the flesh of a Brahmin, the ashes from his funeral pyre, and the earth from that site. (9)
In his right hand he holds a great vajra, and likewise a human head in his left;
white in color and most terrifying, with it he should cut down the wicked. 10.
Every day one should offer a bali-oblation with the nectar of the five meats; and the yogi should constantly pray: "Cut down my enemies! (11)
Having said this, Nipu dies at dawn after seven nights;
or else, those who are afflicted by diseases appear as if overwhelmed by urinary calculi and other ailments.
Having taken the skull of an enemy, one should fill it with human bone;
having filled it, by reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, it wanders like a hungry ghost at the top of a tree.
Now I shall further explain another method, the accomplishment of the great vetāla, which is divine, brings about all accomplishments, and effects various tasks. (14)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Terrible Yamāri," in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
The Tenth Chapter:
[From here, I shall correctly explain the practice for the divine practitioner.]
Desiring repeatedly the means for the accomplishment of a *vetāla*, the practitioner should take a tree-hanging corpse that is unblemished, without wounds, and auspicious;
having brought it down, he should bathe it and recite the mantra there while observing his vow. 1.
Oh, the power of the mantra! Even one who is asleep emits the sound;
when joined with the yoga of Yamāri, one should not fear even in the slightest. // 2 //
Whatever the yogin seeks, all that he obtains—even from a buffalo, a crocodile, or likewise from a tiger. (3)
Especially for a bear, a monkey, or even a dog,
[one should provide] poison, *rājikā* mustard, salt, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and likewise *śobhāñjana*.
By this, one should consecrate an image of Yamāri of terrible form;
the yogin should pray to it and recite the mantra beginning with *hrīḥ ṣṭryā*.
"Give such-and-such a girl to me," [he says]; her father gives her to him.
[He sees] one slain by Yama's enemy being led away in a dream toward the southern direction.
If the father of that [woman] should see her and attempt to lead her astray, the practitioner, observing the vow,
should visualize himself as the three-faced, six-armed, and formidable [deity] holding a mallet.
One should place from the hand a mallet resembling sapphire;
it has three faces, six arms, is wrathful, holds a staff in its hand, and is terrifying. (8)
One should place a staff in his hand— a being who causes even fear to be afraid—
three-faced, six-armed, red in color, and most terrifyingly formidable.
The wise one should visualize in his hand a red lotus called Padma;
he should then visualize Khaḍga, who is dark blue, with three faces and six arms. (10)
Having manifested a sword in the hand, one becomes the performer of all rites;
having manifested a phallus in the womb, one should visualize the Lord of the Maṇḍala. // 11 //
The yogi possessing the recollection of hatred practices the cultivation of the recollection of *hoh*;
relying upon the recollection of delusion, he practices the cultivation of the recollection of slander. (12)
Through the union with the recollection of the female form, one cultivates the recollection of passion;
by means of the yoga of the recollection of passion, the practitioner should bring to mind that which is called envy. (13)
One should emanate clouds of the families from each and every pore;
one should visualize the four wrathful deities situated in the center of a solar mandala.
One should visualize the four goddesses situated in the center of a pure maṇḍala. // 14 //
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the visualization and meditation for the sādhana of Vetāla, in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayamāri-tantra*.
The eleventh chapter:
Having beheld the world overcome by hatred, [he taught] that which brings about the destruction of all hatred.
The Blessed One, out of compassion, assumed the form of the Slayer of Hatred (Dveṣayamāri). // 1 //
Seeing the world overcome by delusion, the Blessed One, out of compassion, manifested the true form of Mohayamāri, which brings about the destruction of all delusion. // 2 //
Seeing the world overcome by slanderers, the Blessed One, out of compassion, assumed the form of the noble Piśnayamāri, the destroyer of all slanderers. // 3 //
Seeing the world overcome by passion, the Blessed One out of compassion assumed the form of Rāgayamāri, which brings about the destruction of all passion. // 4 //
Seeing the world overcome by envy, the Blessed One, out of compassion, assumed the true form of the Slayer of Envy (Īrṣyāyamāri) in order to destroy all envy. (5)
Loving-kindness (maitrī) is said to be Carcikā, and compassion (karuṇā) is likewise Vārāhī;
sympathetic joy (muditā) is Sarasvatī, and equanimity (upekṣā) has the form of Gaurī. // 6 //

Having become fully accomplished within the mandala through one's own entire being, the yogi should emanate [the deities] from the seed-syllable in the heart; he will attain accomplishment, there is no doubt about this. // 7 //
[73] Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the most excellent characteristic of the conduct for the sake of accomplishing the body, speech, and mind of Yamāri, who possesses a terrifying form. 8.
Having mounted a preeminent buffalo in the regions of great forests,
and having made ornaments from snakes, one should carry an iron vajra.
The hair should indeed be made tawny, especially in its upward form;
having wrapped the head with skull-bones, one should maintain a tawny beard.
Having recited the mantra beginning with *hrīḥ ṣṭyā*, one should brandish an iron vajra;
thereafter, the lion’s roar should be performed through the application of Yamārivajra. (11)
Having employed some degree of skill, one may enter the city for sport;
and a beautiful dance should be performed, accompanied by the singing of the ṣāḍava and other melodies.
Then, having seen the street of banners, one should prepare milk there;
with a mind focused on the practice of milk, one should accomplish the Mahāmudrā. // 13 //
Assuming the form of Vārāhī, all women are desired by him;
like a lion, the hero should roam about, accomplishing all desires and purposes. (14)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual preparation for Śatabāhu;
one should prescribe the recitation of his great single-syllable mantra. (15)
One should visualize [the deity] born from the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, with the face of a buffalo;
one should meditate upon him mounted upon a vajra-maṇḍala atop a buffalo. (16)
Whatever weapons and missiles of various forms exist upon the earth,
the wise one should visualize them on the arms during the practice of the mantra in the Māhiṣa rite.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of Daṇḍayamāri;
he whose great mantra is the syllable Hrīḥ and who has a great buffalo as his vehicle. (18)
His body was smeared with ashes, his two arms were each a full hundred thousand *lakṣas* in length,
he was as lofty as Mount Sumeru, and he had completely overspread the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual accomplishment of Kṛtibāhu—the powerful lord, the great mantra with a distorted face, who originates from the syllable HŪṂ. (20)
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ haḥ hāḥ hiḥ hīḥ huḥ hūḥ heḥ haiḥ hoḥ hauḥ haṃ haḥ phaṭ svāhā // 21 //
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing all activities, I shall now describe the practice of the samaya—the blameless and easily obtainable food for one weary of mantra recitation. (22)
[76] Human flesh, and especially the flesh of a horse and an elephant;
as well as that of a cow, a dog, a donkey, a camel, and even a jackal. (23)
Having anointed [the object] with great oil mixed with indigo, one should cook it;
by the mere act of this anointing, one brings the entire world under control. (24)
Rocanā, sinduvāra, and likewise bilva leaves,
along with half the amount of the desired powder, [should be mixed] with the juice of golden leaves.
By rubbing this onto the body, one brings it under the control of the three humors;
indeed, by means of this rubbing, poison, spider-bites, and leprosy are destroyed. (26)
One should drink the great urine as well as the great vajra-nectar;
this is the most excellent and supreme yoga, like drinking the flower of the self-arisen one. (27)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Chapter on the Practice of the Samaya, in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
The Twelfth Chapter.

Then the Blessed One, the Great Being’s Commitment (*mahāpuruṣasamaya*), having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the form of Carcikā, having entered the meditative absorption in the form of Vajravārāhī, having entered the meditative absorption in the form of Sarasvatī, and having entered the meditative absorption in the form of Gaurī, uttered this song of worship: 1.
Aḍeḍe is the nature of the Guru who slays the Kiṭṭaya-demons with blood-red lūvas;
Haḍe is the terrifying nature of the Guru’s wrath, which beholds the world as it truly is. // 2 //
O you who are dancing, why do you dance with such a face as if you were about to die?
Why do you dance with eyes whose collyrium is smudged and a face that has lost its luster? (3)
O Vāmā, you who are called Kālī, you have manifested in many forms;
O daughter of the Thunderbolt-Wielder, I entreat you: dance for the sake of your great bliss! // 4 //
By the mantra *hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ*, dispel whatever deludes the three worlds;
filled with compassion and wrath, act so that the world beholds you. // 5 //
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme characteristics of recitation (jāpa), by means of which application one may attain even greater accomplishment. // 6 //
Neither too fast nor too slow, neither short nor long—while reciting the mantra, the best of men hears nothing at all. (7)
Having taken the bile of a buffalo, a human, an elephant, a cow, a horse, a donkey, or a camel, one should prepare the recitation rosary. 8.
Month by month, on the fourteenth day, one should smear [the image] with the five meats combined with the five nectars; this recitation is supremely efficacious for attaining accomplishment. 9.
At each and every pill, the wise yogi should meditate upon Yamāri;
or else, he should visualize a human head moist with blood. (10)
With merely ten thousand [recitations] of the Bhūtas and a thousand of the Ḍākinīs,
one may slay the multitude of Pretas through the application of Yamamāri.
By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, this soul of yoga accomplishes all its tasks; by ten million recitations, perfection is attained—what need is there to mention fifty million?
Every day, every month, or likewise every year,
a wise person should offer the sixty-four-fold bali-oblation during the sixty-fourth year of life.
Whatever is constantly eaten, whatever is likewise drunk,
or anything else that is consumed— one should offer the very best of it all to Yamāri. 14.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain how one should perform a circumambulation to the Guru, both for one's own peace and for the successful accomplishment of all rites. (15)
One should offer oneself—whether in the form of a horse, a cow, or an elephant—or else grain, gold, a son, or likewise one's own wife. (16)
One should likewise offer one's mother, sister, or even one's niece,
as well as various kinds of garments, an umbrella, or beautiful fly-whisks.
The practitioner under the vow should present to the guru a house, a seat, fragrant substances, song, a vehicle, as well as a sword and ornaments. (18)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Distinction of All Means," in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittakṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, concerning all sentient beings, however many of them may be performers of evil deeds:
Indeed, it is called a "scissors" (*kartarī*) because it cuts through those [afflictions] and the like, and it is a "sheath" (*kośa*) because it severs the afflictions and so forth. // 1 //
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of Vajraḍākinī:
one should visualize the supreme solar mandala situated in the center of the space-element. (2)
Having visualized the five-pronged trident, one should place the foot upon it—[the goddess] who is black in color, most terrifying, six-armed, and beautiful in form. (3)
